Hepatic encephalopathy

Two related rat experiments found improved memory-task performance after transcranial PBM, while brain metabolic responses differed by treatment and region. No clinical evidence was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two related rat experiments found improved memory-task performance after transcranial PBM, while brain metabolic responses differed by treatment and region. No clinical evidence was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

Two related rat experiments from one Spanish research group examined PBM in models linked to minimal hepatic encephalopathy. A 2016 study used portal hypertension as an early encephalopathy model, and a 2021 study compared transcranial PBM with methylene blue in a hepatic-encephalopathy model. They are distinct experiments, not two replications from independent laboratories. No human or cell-culture study was identified in this indication category.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical trial has tested PBM for hepatic encephalopathy in people. The animal outcomes concern memory-task performance and brain metabolism; they do not demonstrate improved liver function, fewer encephalopathy episodes, or better daily functioning in patients.

Animal evidence

In the 2016 experiment, 21 rats were divided among sham, portal-hypertension, and treatment groups. Seven days of 670-nm red LED exposure at 9 J/cm² per day improved stimulus-response task performance compared with untreated portal-hypertension animals. Cytochrome-c-oxidase activity differed across brain regions, while network patterns in treated animals were more similar to sham controls (Arias et al. 2016).

In the 2021 experiment, both PBM and methylene blue improved the experimental memory deficit. Their effects on cytochrome-c-oxidase were not the same: PBM produced lower activity than methylene blue in several analysed regions. Thus, behavioral improvement did not correspond to a uniform increase in this metabolic marker. The two experiments support a possible effect on memory-related behavior in rats, with metabolic responses depending on intervention and brain region (Méndez et al. 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell-culture or ex-vivo study of PBM for hepatic encephalopathy was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2016 study used 670-nm red visible LED applied transcranially once daily for seven days at 9 J/cm². The database identifies transcranial LED treatment in the 2021 study but does not provide a comparably complete dose description. No wavelength or dose comparison was performed. Rat skull transmission and the portal-hypertension model do not establish how much light would reach relevant brain regions in patients.

Interpretation

Both experiments reported better memory-task performance after PBM, so the behavioral direction is favorable within these rat models. The metabolic findings were region-specific rather than uniformly increased, and all studies come from the same research group. The evidence supports additional preclinical testing, not a clinical treatment conclusion.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for short-term memory performance in rat models of minimal hepatic encephalopathy
Publications and records2 related articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two experiments from one Spanish research group reported better stimulus-response memory after transcranial PBM in portal-hypertension rat models. One also compared brain metabolic measures with methylene blue and found different regional effects. No patient study or independent laboratory replication is identified. Replicated animal work and a carefully monitored human feasibility study would be needed to support the next step.
